results.corrected_extracted: As described by the National Academies, four studies compared emissions from e-cigarettes and combustible cigarettes (three laboratory studies and one comparison based on published literature). Using published data and assuming 15 puffs equal one cigarette, selected toxic compounds in smoke were 9- to 450-fold higher than in aerosol (Goniewicz et al., 2014). Of 150 chemicals examined, about 100 were detected in smoke and 16 were generated by one e-cigarette, and toxicants were 82% to more than 99% lower per puff in the aerosol depending on the list and puffing method (Margham et al., 2016). Smoke held about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents than aerosol or room air (Tayyarah and Long, 2014). Of 11 metals with smoke data, the aerosol of one cartomizer was higher for four (aluminium, iron, nickel, sodium), within the smoke range for five and lower for two (Williams et al., 2013). The committee's synthesis: aerosol is substantially less complex than smoke and, except for nicotine, exposure to potentially toxic substances under typical conditions of use is significantly lower (substantial evidence, Conclusion 5-3). The studies are laboratory measurements, not measurements in people.

results.corrected_extracted: As described by the National Academies, studies that followed people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes lasted from 5 days to 8 months; examples: a 12-week trial of 420 people (urinary biomarkers of benzene, acrolein and a nitrosamine fell); a 5-day trial of 105 people (urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower in those who switched partly or completely; exhaled carbon monoxide down 88% to 89% in the groups that switched completely or stopped all nicotine); 20 people over 2 weeks (a nitrosamine breakdown product, NNAL, down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks); and 40 people over 4 weeks (carbon monoxide down 80% in those who only vaped and 52% in those who also smoked). One cross-sectional study compared 181 people who had used these products for a long time, in five groups: nitrosamine and volatile organic compound breakdown products were lower in people who only vaped, or only used nicotine replacement, than in people who smoked, and similar in people who smoked only, vaped and smoked, or used nicotine replacement and smoked (Shahab et al., 2017). Synthesis: all studies showed significantly reduced biomarkers of exposure to potentially toxic chemicals in people who switched, and nicotine intake in people who had stopped smoking and were experienced at vaping was comparable to that from cigarettes. Conclusion 18-1: conclusive evidence that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens (the committee's judgment).

results.note: Counts, sample sizes, results and Conclusion 18-2 match. Fixes: Martin is cross-sectional, a design the Methods exclude from the 15; 'small-airway' is not in the source; 'than cigarettes' added for cell and animal counts.
results.corrected_extracted: As described by the National Academies, the committee found 15 longitudinal observational and cross-over studies of health outcomes in people who switched from cigarettes to e-cigarettes (follow-up from single sessions to about two years; several retrospective record reviews). Examples: a one-year randomised trial of 300 people found no significant differences in lung-function indexes between groups defined by what people did after the trial began, except one flow measure (forced expiratory flow 25-75%) that rose in those who quit smoking, with cough, phlegm and breathlessness falling over follow-up (Cibella et al., 2016); in 15 people white blood cell counts rose after cigarettes but not after e-cigarettes in 30-minute sessions (Flouris et al., 2012); in a cross-over study of 20 adults who smoked and 20 who did not, acute use of either product changed markers of oxidative stress and blood-vessel function, with flow-mediated dilation and vitamin E effects not statistically different between the products and the e-cigarette showing a lesser effect on three other markers (Carnevale et al., 2016); and gingival inflammation increased in 20 people after 2 weeks of vaping instead of smoking (Wadia et al., 2016). A cross-sectional study, a design the Methods say was left out of the 15, compared nasal biopsies from 12 people who vaped, 14 who smoked and 13 who did neither: immune genes suppressed in people who smoked were also suppressed in people who vaped, with more gene changes and stronger suppression (Martin et al., 2016). In cell studies 21 of 27, and in animal studies 3 of 5, favoured e-cigarettes as less harmful than cigarettes and none found them more harmful than cigarettes. Synthesis: health effects of e-cigarettes are still not well understood but current evidence points to them being less harmful than cigarettes; all but one of the human studies showed significant short-term improvements in people who switched, though most studies were small; some studies found similar harm and none found e-cigarettes more harmful among people who switched to exclusive e-cigarette use; whether e-cigarettes reduce health risk still needs support from epidemiological studies and randomised trials. Conclusion 18-2: substantial evidence that completely switching from regular cigarette use to e-cigarettes results in reduced short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems (the committee's judgment).

results.corrected_extracted: The editorial states that in July 2013 a group of 12 experts rated the relative harm of 12 nicotine-containing products on 14 criteria for harm to self and others (reference 1, Nutt et al., 2014, not read), concluding that combustible cigarettes were the most harmful and e-cigarettes substantially less harmful, and that the result was repeated in the popular media as e-cigarettes being 95% less risky or 95% less harmful than combustible cigarettes. It adds that the authors of the 2013 work noted as a limitation the lack of hard evidence for the harms of most products on most of the criteria (quoted from page 224 of that paper); that Public Health England and the Royal College of Physicians endorsed and publicised the assertion; that senior Public Health England staff emphasised the evidence underlying the figure despite its being lacking; and that much was written questioning the figure's validity in 2014 to 2016 (no source cited for the last two). All of this is the authors' account: none of the originals was read.

results.note: Content matches. Fixes: 'less aversive to inhale' is relative to free-base nicotine; reference 4 is cited for protonated-nicotine marketing, so 'no source' was wrong there; bystanders get 'any harmful aerosol constituents'.
results.corrected_extracted: The authors argue that products today differ from those of July 2013 to the extent that the 2013 estimate, even if valid then, can no longer apply: many devices reach a power output 10 to 20 times that of most over-the-counter 2013 models and so make more aerosol, exposing the person vaping to more nicotine and other toxicants and people nearby to more of any harmful aerosol constituents, and raising the chance of malfunction; there are thousands of flavours whose lung toxicity is unknown; and liquids with protonated nicotine (nicotine salt) are widely marketed and, relative to free-base nicotine, are less aversive to inhale, which the authors say allows higher nicotine concentrations and likely more dependence. No source is cited in the text for the statements on power, flavours or dependence; reference 4 (Jackler and Ramamurthi, 2019, not read) is cited for the marketing of protonated nicotine liquids and the 'nicotine arms race'; the online Appendix A, a nonexhaustive list of evidence of harm, was not read.

Matches except one dropped hedge: the source says toxicants 'sometimes differ' from cigarette smoke. No citation in the paragraph and no size estimate, as the anchor says.
results.corrected_extracted: The authors argue that differences in toxicant content between aerosol and smoke, by themselves, cannot show lesser lethality, because toxicity depends on the extent and mode of use; that propylene glycol is toxic when injected over days and that aerosols containing it and glycerol cause inflammation in human lungs (no source cited); and that, because the toxicants sometimes differ, so might the diseases. They also state that there is little doubt that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines or polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, largely absent from the aerosol, and that what diseases they may die of, and whether use hastens death, will be part of the evidence needed for valid risk estimates. The editorial offers no estimate of the size of the difference.

Source says adjustment is unlikely to 'fully' overcome confounding, 'particularly for the health conditions most affected by smoking'; both restored. 'Useful when discussing' the minority who quit completely, not 'useful for' them (reads as advice).
results.corrected_extracted: The review states that e-cigarettes are relatively new, diverse and changing rapidly, that long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current options (limited information on newer nicotine salt products). It describes confounding between the effects of e-cigarette use and of smoking as a major problem that statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully overcome, particularly for the health conditions most affected by smoking, because older people who vape generally smoke regularly, are trying to quit or have quit, while younger people who vape often do not smoke regularly; it concludes that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to quantify the effects of e-cigarettes and that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group. Statements that e-cigarettes are safer than smoking, and terms such as tobacco harm reduction, may be useful when discussing the minority of people who smoke who use e-cigarettes to quit completely but are not applicable to people who do not smoke; comparisons with the effects of smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

results.note: The source gives the reason for 'unlikely to have large effects': significant concerns in other domains meant bias risks mattered less. Without it, the sentence reads as reassurance about bias. Reason added; rest matches.
results.corrected_extracted: The review rated the certainty of evidence very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes. It notes that the tobacco and related industries can influence research, so its risk-of-bias assessment took account of competing interests such as financial support from tobacco or pharmaceutical industries; it writes that risks of bias were noted across health outcomes, but significant concerns in other domains meant they were unlikely to have large effects on its interpretation or the overall certainty of evidence. It states that it applies the precautionary principle (exposure to an agent with uncertain effects to be avoided), which it considers appropriate when serious adverse impacts are scientifically plausible, particularly those affecting future generations. Products not reported as nicotine or non-nicotine were assumed to be largely nicotine e-cigarettes (Box 3 note).

results.corrected_extracted: Meta-analyses of 25 longitudinal studies found strong evidence that young people who have never smoked and who use e-cigarettes are about three times as likely as those who do not to start smoking tobacco and to go on to smoke regularly (residual confounding cannot be excluded; the review deemed the link likely causal on Bradford-Hill criteria); limited evidence that people who had stopped smoking and use e-cigarettes are about twice as likely to resume smoking. The review names this, with poisoning, dependence (addiction) and toxicity from inhalation, among the risks that disproportionately affect people who do not smoke and young people. This concerns the harm of starting to smoke, a different comparison from vaping against smoking, and the UK review left it out of its scope.
